claim: Pick big, already-understood categories where every incumbent looks the same, then import a cultural shift the category has missed; the business sits in the gap between.
body: Ryan's screening model has three signals, all observable by walking the aisle. First, size and familiarity: an existing large category means no consumer education, so a 'saturated' shelf is a plus, not a minus. Second, a sea of sameness: every pack looks alike (all dish soaps green and toxic-looking, all vitamins round, pseudo-scientific or folksy). Two extra clues that a category is ripe: it takes itself too seriously, or it is needlessly complicated (vitamins sold by ingredient so shoppers ask strangers what magnesium is for). Third, a cultural shift already visible in a different category that has not reached this one: for Method it was home lifestyling plus health and sustainability, for Olly it was the way SoulCycle turned fitness into a lifestyle pursuit. The product is the intersection of familiar and novel. Olly's execution shows the moves: since every competitor was round, the jar became square; the cap became the logo; SKUs were named by benefit (Sleep, Beauty) instead of ingredient (melatonin, biotin); the jar was designed to be left on the counter, which also helps people remember to take it. How to apply: photograph the shelf, list the shared cues, list shifts happening in adjacent lifestyle categories, and only proceed if one shift clearly has not reached this aisle.
conditions: Mass consumer categories sold at retail or DTC where packaging and shelf presence drive choice; founder can design and brand; physical products bought repeatedly.
fails_when: The category is small or the sameness exists because of regulation or cost (commodity price buyers who ignore design); the 'shift' is a niche trend that has not reached mainstream buyers; B2B or spec-driven purchases where design is not a purchase driver.
numbers: Method and Olly each described as near $0.5B to $1B brands
asks: How do I find a product category worth disrupting?
Is a crowded, saturated category a bad place to launch a new brand?
Every brand in my aisle looks the same. Is that an opportunity?
What signs tell me a boring category is ripe for a new brand?

evidence.quote: they're all round so we had no choice but to be square

claim: When reinventing a commodity product, change exactly one major variable from what shoppers expect; changing two or three at once usually makes it too novel to adopt.
body: Eric Ryan (Method, Olly, Welly) calls this his golden rule, borrowed from apparel and fashion: one iteration off the category core has a high hit rate, while two or three simultaneous changes usually fail. The mechanism is adoption cost. A shopper can absorb one surprise (a dish soap that looks like a vase, a vitamin that is a gummy, a bandage with a pattern) while every other cue still says the product works as expected. Stack several changes and the shopper must re-learn the category, which needs education budget most launches do not have. His own counter-example: a 10x concentrated laundry detergent in a shampoo-sized bottle that did 50 loads with a pre-measured pump. It was technically better but failed because buyers had been trained that a big jug is what cleans clothes. He says he has failed far more often by being too novel than too familiar. How to apply: list every attribute buyers expect (format, size, dose, colour, price band, channel, claim) and pick the one to change; hold the rest at category norm; if the concept needs two changes, launch one now and keep the second for a later SKU. The same rule applies to messaging: lead with one difference, not four.
conditions: Entering an established, large consumer category where buyers already understand the product; retail or DTC CPG; brand without a large consumer-education budget.
fails_when: The category is genuinely new and buyers must be educated anyway, or the single change is cosmetic and gives no reason to switch; well-funded launches that can pay for education (or regulated innovation like a new active ingredient) can carry more novelty.
numbers: 1 variable changed from category core vs 2 to 3 (likely failure), practitioner rule
10x concentrated detergent, shampoo-size bottle for 50 loads: failed launch

claim: A single viral hero product decays: Oodie peaked near $200M a year with only about $5M from other products, then declined faster than its 20%-a-year secondary range grew.
body: Oodie reached roughly $200M in annual revenue in its third year, but almost all of it came from one product, the wearable blanket, with only about $5M from anything else. After the peak, revenue slid to about $190M and then $180M as competitors arrived, the trend fatigued and the pandemic lift reverted. The founder's later fix was to define the brand by the function the hero serves (comfort), then add more evergreen secondary products: nightwear, dressing gowns, bath hoodies, forecast at about $50M for the year and growing near 20% a year for three to four years. Even so, the hero was declining faster than the range was growing. The lesson for expansion planning: start the secondary range while the hero is still rising, not after it peaks, because a 20% growth rate on a small base cannot cover a fast-falling hero. He also says stockouts cost Oodie an estimated 30 to 50% more revenue at the peak. Founder recall, approximate numbers, one brand.
conditions: Brand whose revenue is concentrated in one trend-driven or viral hero SKU; the hero is still growing or near peak.
fails_when: The hero is a staple with steady replenishment demand rather than a trend; the brand already has a broad catalogue; adding SKUs would spread scarce cash and inventory too thin before the hero is stable.

revenue then about $190M and $180M in following years
secondary range forecast about $50M, growing about 20% a year for 3 to 4 years
stockouts estimated to cost 30 to 50% extra revenue at the peak

claim: Screen new products for a $50 to $150 retail price; a candidate that can only sell at $9 to $20 struggles to fund paid acquisition at launch.
body: The reason for the band is unit economics on paid traffic. Below roughly $50, the profit per order is too thin to absorb a customer acquisition cost from paid ads, especially before bulk pricing lowers unit cost. Above roughly $150, buyers hesitate to purchase from an unknown online store and start expecting premium service such as phone support, which raises operating cost. In the source's worked example, a coconut hair mask passed demand checks (about 73,000 monthly Google searches, about 150 daily tweets, rising Google Trends interest, scarce in physical stores) but comparable products sold for only $9 to $20 per 120 ml, which the presenter flagged as the first red flag because paid channels would be hard to make work at launch. How to apply: price two dozen comparable products first, take the realistic selling range, and check whether the margin at the low end can cover a plausible first-purchase CAC. If not, the product needs a bundle, a larger format, repeat purchase or an organic channel to work. The band is a heuristic attributed to experienced ecommerce operators, not measured data.
conditions: New single-brand DTC store relying on paid ads for first purchases; product candidate screening before inventory commitment.
fails_when: Low-priced consumables with strong repeat purchase, bundles or subscriptions that lift first-order value, or brands with organic or marketplace demand that does not pay a per-order CAC; luxury or high-consideration categories where buyers expect to pay well above $150.
numbers: $50 to $150 retail price band for paid-acquisition products
$9 to $20 per 120 ml comparable price range in the worked example
about 73,000 monthly searches and 150 tweets per day in the worked example

claim: Line extensions survive only while a category has no strong rival; run the shopping-list test: if your name on a list could mean several products, the brand is diluting.
body: The authors' test for line extension: write the brand name alone on a shopping list and send someone to buy it. If they come back with the intended product without asking, the brand still owns a position (Kleenex, Bayer, Dial at the time). If the name could mean several products (Heinz pickles or ketchup, Scott tissue or towels), the brand is losing meaning. A spoken version is the bartender test: order by brand and see if you get what you meant. The damage is slow, often taking years. Kraft is the worked example: the brand was on many categories but led almost none, while the company's category leaders carried other names (Philadelphia, Sealtest, Parkay). Kraft still won in cheese only because the category had weak competition, and the authors warn an extension holds only until a strong specialist arrives. Cost examples: Sara Lee lost about $8 million on frozen entrees; Saturday Review lost $17 million splitting into four editions. Before extending, ask whether a focused specialist could enter that category; if so, use a separate name or skip it.
conditions: A brand with a clear core product considering adding products in other categories.
fails_when: Categories bought without brand preference, or with no strong specialists, where a known name beats unknown ones.

Saturday Review four-edition loss $17 million

claim: Put a new product under the house brand only if it is low-volume, in a crowded field, lightly advertised, a commodity, or rep-sold; otherwise give it its own name.
body: Ries and Trout give five rules for deciding when a new product should carry the existing brand name and when it needs a new one. 1. Expected volume: a potential big winner should get its own name; small-volume items can ride the house name. 2. Competition: entering an empty category, use a new name so it can own the category; entering a crowded field, the familiar house name helps. 3. Advertising support: big-budget launches should carry a new name; small-budget products benefit from borrowed recognition. 4. Significance: a breakthrough deserves its own name; commodity items do not. 5. Distribution: products picked off a shelf by the shopper need their own name; products sold through sales reps can carry the house name. The logic is that one name standing for two different things blurs the position of both, but many products are bought without any prior brand preference, and there a known name beats an unknown one. Apply it before naming a new SKU line: score the launch on the five rules. Mostly-new-name answers mean a separate brand; mostly-house-name answers mean a line extension is acceptable.
conditions: Deciding brand architecture for a new product or category entry; strongest for a brand moving into a category different from its core.
fails_when: Variants within the same category (new size, flavour, colour) where the shopper already expects one brand; and very small brands that cannot afford to build a second name at all.
numbers: 5 rules: expected volume, competition, advertising support, significance, distribution

claim: First-run beverage brands can cut packaging minimums about tenfold by using sleeve-wrapped cans instead of printed cans; treat printed packaging as a nice-to-have.
body: McKay separates must-haves from nice-to-haves when de-risking a product launch. Cadence chose printed cans, which carry much higher minimum order quantities, because the brand is built on a premium positioning. For founders without that capital or certainty, he says a sleeve can (a blank can with a shrink sleeve label) carries roughly a tenth of the MOQ of a printed can, and most startup beverages begin there. The same logic applies beyond drinks: decoration methods that can be applied late (labels, sleeves, stickers, inserts) let you run small batches, change claims after regulators or retailers push back, and avoid writing off thousands of printed units when a rebrand happens (Cadence rebranded three times in about 300 days). He also notes most founders start with a manufacturer's stock formula and add their label, which is fine for speed, while Cadence used a formulator for a custom product. How to apply: list every packaging and formulation choice, mark which ones the customer would actually notice at launch, and choose the low-MOQ version for the rest until velocity is proven.
conditions: New consumable products, pre-product-market-fit, cash-constrained first production runs.
fails_when: Premium positioning depends on the finish (Cadence's own choice), or a retailer requires printed packaging; at scale, where sleeve unit cost exceeds printed unit cost.
numbers: sleeve can MOQ about one tenth of a printed can MOQ

claim: Judge retail launches by units per store per week, not door count; retailers review every 30 days, and beverage can turn 10 to 20 units versus 1 in slow categories.
body: McKay argues that door count is a vanity metric: being in 10,000 stores means nothing if each store sells one unit a week. Retail buyers track velocity, measured as units per store per week and dollars per store per week, and in his experience a brand effectively wins or loses its shelf in 30-day cycles: after each 30 days the data comes back and the brand adjusts price, adds a promotion such as two-for-$4, or loses space. Fast categories carry higher expectations because the space next to you turns quickly. His modelling method is bottom-up: units per store per week times stores times 52 times price. At 10 to 20 units a week per store across 3,000 stores of one account, a single flavour is roughly a $20M line, which is how beverage brands reach very large numbers; his previous category turned about one unit a week, which made the same door count a small business. How to apply: before taking a retail deal, find the category's typical velocity, model revenue from velocity rather than doors, and budget trial-driving promotion for the first 30 to 90 days, since the first review decides the next order.
conditions: Brick-and-mortar retail expansion, especially grocery and convenience consumables with high purchase frequency; US mass retail.
fails_when: Slow-turn categories (home goods, durable goods) where low weekly velocity is normal and buyers judge on margin per square foot instead; online-only marketplaces where store counts do not apply.

slow category: about 1 unit per store per week

claim: McKay's rule for retail CPG: put all capital behind one hero SKU until it reaches about $10M before launching the next, while still showing retailers 2 to 3 flavours.
body: McKay warns that each new SKU spreads a small team thin: new manufacturers, terms, volumes, forecasting and retailer conversations. His rule is that until the hero SKU is doing around $10M, there is no point launching the next flavour, because capital and attention behind the winner compound while a second product dilutes both. Two nuances keep this from being absolute. First, retailers want to see two or three options, so Cadence launched with a few flavours of the same product rather than one. Second, Cadence did launch 13 SKUs in about 18 months, but 90% of focus stays on the canned drink, and the rest are high-margin, subscription-heavy DTC items (sachets around 65% subscription) that keep the brand grounded with its core athletes. He also advises keeping new products with the same production facility where possible, because each extra manufacturer is another relationship to manage. How to apply: name one hero SKU, set a revenue milestone before the next launch, allow flavour or size variants only where the channel demands choice, and treat side products as audience-serving, not growth bets.
conditions: Consumer packaged goods brands entering retail with limited team and capital; hero-product categories.
fails_when: Fashion, beauty colour or other assortment-driven categories where breadth is the product; DTC brands whose growth comes from cross-sell and repeat on a range; the $10M figure is one founder's threshold, not a benchmark.

claim: Ridge screens products in order: can it win new customers (over $50, big market, not an add-on)? Does it lift repeat purchase? Does it sell on Amazon or wholesale?
body: Ridge's wallet business is about $100M a year, but wallet buyers rarely need a second wallet, so repeat revenue was weak; over half the business now comes from other products, and the goal is returning-customer revenue at 50%. Frank's three-step screen: First, is it a CAC product or an LTV product? A CAC product can win new customers through paid ads: priced above about $50, a large market, and not a complement to something already sold (a key case that pairs with the wallet cannot be advertised to strangers, so it is LTV only and sold to the base). Second, what does it do for LTV across the range? Luggage buyers turned out likely to buy wallets. Third, is there a distribution play beyond DTC, such as Amazon or wholesale? Phone cases ($40 to $75) passed all three: competitive in the ad auction, strong cross-sell with wallets, and good on Amazon and at Best Buy. Treat launches as lottery tickets: watches, mini knives and apparel failed, and he advises dropping flops rather than forcing them with more marketing. Yeti's cooler is now under 20% of revenue, with drinkware about 70%.
conditions: Brand expanding beyond a low-repeat hero product; performance-marketing-led acquisition; Ridge, US, about $100M+ revenue.
fails_when: Consumables or replenishment brands where repeat is already high; brands without cash to absorb failed launches; products under about $50 that cannot carry paid CAC.

claim: Screen new products for repeat purchase, parcel-friendly packaging and 'for me or for you' gifting demand; cans and large frames are hard to ship profitably.
body: The guest's product criteria after selling hoverboards, fidget spinners and now a cannabis-infused drink: the product should change how the buyer feels or behaves in a way they notice each use, which drives repeat purchase (his examples: electrolyte packets and unbranded colognes); it should ship small, ideally in a parcel or sleeve that can be fulfilled at volume, since cans and large framed items are expensive and fragile to ship; and it should be a 'for me or for you' product that people buy for themselves and others buy for them, like baby products or cookware that lands on gift lists. Packaging is a margin lever: his team expected a per-unit saving from moving to a four-pack, and redesigned cans because too many arrived crushed, spending more per unit to cut breakage. For expansion into retail, study how the category is merchandised on the shelf; he notes shelf lines often run in threes (original, sugar-free, a flavour). How to apply: score candidates on repeat cycle, shipping dimensions and weight, breakage risk, and gifting potential before sampling.
conditions: New product selection or line extension for DTC brands shipping by parcel.
fails_when: Durable one-off products sold on high margin, where repeat purchase is not the model; categories where bulk or fragile formats are the point and freight is priced in.
numbers: retail shelf lines often in threes

claim: IM8 sells 100% DTC to 31 countries (98% own site, 2% Amazon), only 40% from the US, and is declining retail for about 3 more years.
body: Rather than pairing US DTC with US retail, IM8 went international DTC from day one. It ships to 31 countries; the US is only about 40% of revenue, followed by Canada, the UK, Australia and Hong Kong. Sales are 100% direct to consumer, 98% on its own site and 2% on Amazon. Every major retailer has approached the brand and been declined; the founder expects at least three more years before serious retail talks. His reasons: growth headroom in DTC markets is still large, adding retail now would cost focus, and the team cannot do everything well at this stage. The host adds that repeatedly declining retailers improves the eventual terms. International DTC suits a subscription model with prepaid multi-month plans and premium global partners, and spreads concentration away from one market. How to apply: before entering retail, test whether new DTC countries can add revenue at your target payback (shipping, duties and local pricing included); keep Amazon minimal if site subscription economics are better; set an explicit date or revenue threshold for revisiting retail rather than reacting to inbound offers.
conditions: High-margin, light, shippable consumables with strong site subscription economics; brands with global awareness from partnerships.
fails_when: Heavy or low-margin products where cross-border shipping and duties kill payback; categories where retail presence drives trust and trial; brands whose buyers prefer Amazon, making a minimal Amazon presence a lost channel.

claim: Google Trends scores are a sample of searches divided by all searches in that place and time, then scaled 0 to 100; they show relative interest and direction, not how many people search.
body: Google's Trends FAQ says Trends uses a sample of Google searches. Each data point is divided by the total searches of the geography and time range it represents, to compare relative popularity, and the result is scaled on a range of 0 to 100 based on the topic's proportion of all searches. Google adds that regions showing the same search interest do not always have the same total search volume. How to apply: use Trends to read direction (rising, flat, falling), seasonality and which regions over-index, always over the same time range and region when comparing terms; never quote a Trends score as a count of buyers, and get volume from Keyword Planner, Merchant Center or marketplace data instead.
conditions: Any market where Google is the main search engine, including India and the US.
fails_when: Very low-volume terms show zeros or spikes from sampling; buyers in the niche search mostly on Amazon, Flipkart or TikTok rather than Google.
numbers: scale 0 to 100

claim: Merchant Center's free Popular products tab ranks products and brands on Google by how often people search for or buy them, by category and country (India and the US included), with brand rank change and price range, refreshed weekly.
body: Google's help page says the Popular products tab in Merchant Center Analytics shows cards for popular products, popular brands, brands gaining popularity, top-selling products and out-of-stock products the merchant might restock. Popularity is ranked by how often customers search for or buy the items, and a smaller rank number means more popular. Brand rank change shows how far a brand has risen against an earlier period, and price range shows current prices for a product across Google. Results filter by category and cover 36 countries including India, the United States and the United Kingdom. Data updates weekly, though new data can take up to two weeks to appear. Cards with product suggestions may be hidden if Google decides the merchant sells only its own products, and the data is for internal use only: it cannot be resold, shown publicly or aggregated across businesses. How to apply: a free Merchant Center account gives a store a first-party list of rising products and brands in its category to screen, without a paid spy tool.
conditions: Stores with a Merchant Center account selling in one of the 36 listed countries.
fails_when: The category is too small to rank, the store sells only its own brand (suggestion cards can be hidden), or the products sell mainly on marketplaces and social shops rather than through Google.

claim: Merchant Center's Pricing tab gives a benchmark price per product, built from every retailer selling the same GTIN on Shopping ads and free listings, and the store's price gap against it; it needs a valid GTIN.
body: Google's help page says the benchmark is the average price that typically leads to more successful ad auctions, impressions, clicks or conversions, depending on available data, and it is calculated from the prices of all retailers selling a product with the same GTIN across Shopping ads and organic listings. The report shows how many of the store's products are cheaper or dearer than benchmark, the price gap as a percentage difference between the store's price and the benchmark, the price distribution and the products with the highest gaps. A valid GTIN is needed for benchmark data; sale price suggestions are a separate feature that needs purchase conversions reported. How to apply: for branded or resold products with GTINs, use the price gap report as the free weekly feed for rival price tracking; own-brand products with unique GTINs will have no rival benchmark, so track named rivals by hand.
conditions: Products with valid GTINs listed in Merchant Center.
fails_when: Private-label products with no shared GTIN, or categories where few retailers list on Google.

body: Meta's Transparency Center says the Ad Library lets anyone search ads currently running across Meta technologies. Ads about social issues, elections or politics are shown whether active or inactive and are stored for seven years, with spend, reach and funding entity. Ads that delivered impressions in the EU are archived for one year after their last impression. A separate database shows active branded content carrying a paid partnership label. Ad presence or run length is a proxy, never proof of profit.

claim: Size Amazon demand by niche, not by one keyword: Product Opportunity Explorer groups the search terms whose shoppers click and buy the same products, and shows search volume, click share and conversion per term.
body: Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer, available to Professional sellers in Seller Central under Growth, is built to judge unmet demand for new product ideas. Its unit is the niche: a cluster of customer search terms that lead to the same products being viewed and bought (stainless-steel water bottle, BPA-free water bottle and insulated water bottle form one niche), titled by the highest-volume term. Each niche has a Products tab with the top clicked and purchased products, their launch dates, click share, price, average Amazon fees and trends, and a Search terms tab with search volume, click share, search conversion and the top three clicked products per term. Searching works by keyword, category or ASIN, and the store can be switched from the US default. Amazon warns the data is a guide and not a promise of sales. Because a niche merges all the ways shoppers describe one need, its total volume is a better demand estimate than any single keyword from a third-party tool, and its term list shows which descriptions (size, material, use) matter. How to apply: for each idea, open its niche, record total search volume, the click share held by the top three products and how recent their launch dates are, and compare ideas on the same three numbers.
conditions: Professional seller account; product ideas sold or sellable on Amazon (US by default, other stores selectable).
numbers: top 3 clicked products shown per search term

claim: Read saturation in Product Opportunity Explorer's Insights tab, which gives 20 data points over today, 90 and 360 days, including product count, top-clicked products and a low share of Prime offers.
body: The Insights tab of Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer analyses a niche through 20 data points across three time frames: today, the past 90 days and the past 360 days. Amazon points to two uses: the number of products and the concentration among top-clicked products show how saturated the niche is, and a low percentage of Prime products signals room for a new offer with Prime delivery. The Trends tab plots up to two metrics at a time over time (each point aggregates the previous seven days), with up to five metrics kept in the picker, which shows whether search volume and product count are growing together or whether new products are arriving faster than demand. Comparing the 90-day and 360-day columns separates a niche that is filling up quickly from one that has been stable for a year. How to apply: for each shortlisted niche, note product count today against 360 days ago, the share of clicks taken by the top products, and the Prime share; prefer niches where demand grew faster than product count and where the leaders' click share is not locked up, and treat a fast-rising product count with flat search volume as a warning.
conditions: Professional seller account; niches with enough history for 360-day data.
numbers: 20 data points

claim: Mine a niche's reviews and returns before designing the product: Product Opportunity Explorer groups review themes with their effect on star rating, and lists the most common return reasons as a share of returns.
body: Two tabs in Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer do the review and return mining a founder would otherwise do by hand. The Returns tab lists the most common buyer reasons for returning products in the niche, each as a percentage of all returns, with trends over time, taken from buyer feedback. claim: Product Opportunity Explorer's Purchase drivers tab ranks up to 10 product features by how much they raise or lower units sold in a niche, compared with the niche average, which tells you which spec to build.
body: Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer includes a Purchase drivers tab that shows the features most linked to higher or lower sales in a niche. Amazon calculates impact by comparing estimated sales of products that have a feature with the average units sold for all products in the niche, and shows up to 10 of the most relevant positive or negative features. Features are pulled from product names, descriptions and bullet points and tagged by theme where one applies, such as color: blue in a T-shirt niche. The tab turns spec choices (size, material, pack count, a function) into evidence from what shoppers actually bought, rather than guesses. It reflects correlation in existing listings, so a feature can look strong because the leading brand happens to have it. How to apply: before briefing a factory, list the positive drivers your product will have and the negative ones it must avoid, check the strongest driver against review themes to see whether shoppers mention it, and write the top driver into the title and main image.

claim: When comparing ideas in Google Trends, compare topics rather than single terms where possible; terms miss misspellings, synonyms and plural forms, while a topic groups one concept across terms and languages.
body: Google's Trends help on comparing terms sets the rules. The current Explore lets a user compare up to 8 groups of terms at once, with up to 50 terms in each group (classic Explore allows 5 groups of 25). A search term matches the words typed in the chosen language: one word also returns phrases containing it, several words return results containing each word in any order, and quotation marks restrict results to the exact phrase. The plus sign combines terms into one line, such as two languages for the same word. Terms do not pick up misspellings, spelling variations, synonyms, or plural and singular versions, so a single term can understate interest. Topics are groups of terms sharing one concept in any language, for example London including Londres. Non-Latin terms may return little data where most people search in English. How to apply: compare product ideas as topics when Trends offers one; when it does not, build a group with the plural, singular and common synonyms joined by plus signs, keep the same region and time range for every idea, and read the shape of the line (rising, flat, seasonal), not its absolute value.
conditions: Google Trends comparisons for any country.

classic Explore: 5 groups, 25 terms each

claim: A Google Trends line at or near 0 means too little search volume to show, and low-interest lines are mostly noise; do not read a spike in a tiny niche term as rising demand.
body: Google's Trends FAQ explains why small terms behave badly. Trends only shows data for popular terms, so terms with low search volume appear as 0. Because the data is a sample of searches, some noise is always present, and Google says it is most noticeable on queries with low or no search interest, where lines jump around for random reasons. Trends also removes repeated searches from the same person over a short time and filters out queries with apostrophes and other special characters. Graphs for 30 days or longer use UTC with daily, weekly or monthly points, while seven days or less use local time and hourly points. For product research this means a niche idea whose Trends line is mostly zeros with occasional spikes has no readable trend at all, and a single spike is likely noise, not a breakout. How to apply: before trusting a Trends signal, widen to the broader topic or category term and a multi-year window; if the specific term is still mostly 0, size demand with a volume tool (Keyword Planner, Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer) instead, and only call a trend when the line rises across several periods.
conditions: Google Trends for niche or long-tail product terms.

claim: Keyword Planner's average monthly searches is a 12-month average for the exact keyword and close variants, rounded, so add variants yourself and read it as an order of magnitude.
body: Google's Keyword Planner help defines average monthly searches as the average number of times people searched for a keyword and its close variants, for the chosen month range, location and Search Network settings; by default it is averaged over 12 months. Historical statistics such as average monthly searches are shown only for exact matches, and traffic forecasts account for match types while historical volume does not. Volumes are rounded, so totals across locations may not add up. A 12-month average hides seasonality: a product searched heavily in winter and barely in summer gets one middling number. Very low volume terms are not shown at all. For product research this makes Keyword Planner a good tool for comparing the rough scale of ideas and a poor one for precise forecasts. How to apply: for each idea, list the main term plus its common synonyms and long-tail variants, sum their average monthly searches in the target country, check the monthly breakdown for seasonality, and compare ideas on that sum, treating small differences as a tie.

claim: Estimate a new product's paid-search click cost from Keyword Planner's top-of-page bid range: the low end is about the 20th percentile of past bids and the high end the 80th, over the last 30 days.
body: Google's Keyword Planner help explains the bid columns: top of page bid (low range) is roughly the 20th percentile of bids advertisers paid to show at the top of the page, and the high range roughly the 80th percentile, both from the last 30 days of bid data. Forecasts of clicks and conversions take bid, budget, seasonality and historical ad quality into account and are built from about a week of data, so day-to-day numbers vary. At the idea stage, this gives a cost per click for the product's main terms before any money is spent. Divide that click cost by an assumed conversion rate to get an ad cost per order before fees and product cost, then compare it with the gross profit per order. If the high-range bid on the core terms already eats most of the margin, paid search cannot fund the launch. How to apply: pull top-of-page bid ranges for the core terms of each idea, use the high end for a cautious case, and drop ideas where the cost per order at a modest conversion rate leaves too little of the gross profit per order to fund the business.

claim: In the US, a smoke test that takes orders for a product you may never make must follow the FTC's dry-testing conditions: say it is only planned and may not ship, notify buyers if dropped, refund promptly and never substitute.
body: The FTC's guide to the Mail, Internet or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule covers testing demand for merchandise that does not exist yet, which it calls dry-testing. A seller may do it only if five conditions are met: the promotion makes no suggestion that the item will be shipped or that interested customers will receive it; every promotional material discloses all material aspects, including that the merchandise is only planned and may not be shipped; if any part of the promotion is later dropped, buyers are told within a reasonable time; if no decision to ship has been made within a reasonable time, buyers are told and offered the chance to cancel, with a prompt refund where they paid; and no other merchandise is substituted for what was ordered. If the conditions are not met, the full rule applies, with its shipping deadlines. A fake buy button that takes money with no disclosure is not a smoke test under this guidance; it is an order. How to apply: run demand tests as a clearly labelled waitlist or reservation (planned product, may not ship, refundable), collect emails or deposits only on those terms, and set a decision date after which you either ship or refund everyone.
conditions: US buyers; online, mail or phone orders.

claim: US pre-orders must ship within the time you state, or 30 days if you state none; when late, get the buyer's consent to a new date or refund within seven working days of cancellation.
body: The FTC's Mail, Internet or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule applies to pre-orders once money is taken. A seller must ship within the time clearly stated or, with no statement, within 30 days of receiving a properly completed order (payment plus the information needed), and must have a reasonable basis for any shipping promise, based on expected demand, supply, fulfilment capacity and records. When the seller learns it cannot ship on time, it must seek the buyer's consent to the delay before the promised date; a first delay notice with a new date of 30 days or less can treat silence as consent. If consent is not obtained, the seller must refund all money for unshipped goods without being asked. Refunds are due within seven working days after cancellation, or within one billing cycle for credit sales where the seller is the creditor. Factory delays are common on a first production run, so a pre-order campaign with a tight ship date turns a supplier slip into a legal deadline. How to apply: state a ship window that includes production, freight and inspection plus buffer, write the delay-notice email before launch, and keep a cash reserve to refund every pre-order if the run fails.
conditions: US buyers; online, mail or phone orders of physical goods.

claim: Amazon says ACOS must stay below the profit margin to make money, so an idea's margin before ads is its break-even ACOS; at ACOS times price you know the ad cost each ad-driven order can bear.
body: Amazon Ads' ACOS guide states that to maintain a profit, ACOS needs to be lower than the profit margin, and that the first step is working out break-even ACOS before setting a target. ACOS is ad spend divided by ad sales. That turns into a screen at the idea stage. Take the target price; subtract landed product cost, marketplace or payment fees, fulfilment and an allowance for returns; the share left is the margin before advertising, which is also the break-even ACOS. Whatever share that is, each ad-attributed order can carry ad spend up to that share of the price before the sale loses money. If research suggests launch campaigns in the niche will run near or above that level, the product only works if organic and repeat sales carry it. Amazon adds that new campaigns often show high ACOS simply because they are new. How to apply: for every shortlisted idea, compute margin before ads at the target price, write it down as break-even ACOS, and drop or re-price ideas whose break-even sits below the ACOS you expect during launch.
conditions: Products sold with paid ads on Amazon or elsewhere; any marketplace.

From 15 January 2027 the bulky tier splits into four and extra-large into six oversize tiers, smaller and lighter items paying less. Dangerous goods pay higher bulky rates again. The highest include backpacks, handbags and luggage at 12.8%, compact appliances 12.6%, eyewear 12.1%, watches 12.0%, full-size appliances 11.9%, computers 11.4%, consumer electronics 11.2%, jewellery 10.8% and pet products 10.2%. claim: Big parcels carry carrier surcharges on Amazon's US return labels: UPS adds handling over 50 pounds or 48 inches, and a large package surcharge with a 90-pound minimum billable weight past 96 inches long or 130 inches length plus girth.
body: Amazon's page on seller-fulfilled return shipping costs passes on carrier rules that make bulky products expensive to take back. UPS bills the greater of actual or dimensional weight (length times width times height divided by 139 inches) plus a fuel charge that typically runs 13% to 15%. An additional handling surcharge can apply when a package weighs more than 50 pounds or its longest side exceeds 48 inches. A large package surcharge applies when the longest side exceeds 96 inches or length plus girth (twice the width plus twice the height) exceeds 130 inches, and such packages have a minimum billable weight of 90 pounds. Adjustments can post two to three weeks later. For product research this is a second cost of size beyond outbound fulfilment: each return of a big, light product is billed on box volume, not weight. How to apply: for any idea in a large box, compute its dimensional weight at the 139 divisor, check it against the surcharge limits, and cost an expected return label into the margin; a product that crosses 48 inches or 50 pounds needs either a high price or a near-zero return reason.

claim: A seasonal product stocked at Amazon for winter pays peak storage: $2.40 per cubic foot a month for standard items in October to December against $0.78 in January to September.
body: Amazon's storage fee page shows how much the calendar matters for seasonal products. Before the February 2027 change, standard-size items pay a base of $0.78 per cubic foot per month in the off-peak period (January to September) and $2.40 in the peak period (October to December); oversize items pay $0.56 and $1.40. Sellers past their first year with high storage utilization pay a surcharge on top, up to a total of $4.28 per cubic foot in peak for standard items. A product whose demand peaks in winter is therefore stored at the much higher peak rate exactly when it is needed, and anything left after the season sits into the next year as aged stock, which the new age-based fee charges more for after six months. For product research, a strongly seasonal idea needs a margin that covers peak storage and an exit plan for leftovers. How to apply: read the idea's Trends line over several years to time the peak, plan to land stock just before it, size the order to sell through within the season, and plan a markdown or removal for the remainder before it ages.
conditions: Amazon US FBA storage before 1 February 2027; age-based rates after that.

It names three supplier identifiers: Gold Supplier; Verified Supplier, whose profile, management system and production capability have been assessed or inspected by third parties; and Trade Assurance suppliers, who accept payment through Alibaba.com's payment portal. The guide advises keeping the transaction on Alibaba.com, mentions its Product Inspection Services, and recommends ordering samples, especially for private label or customised products, before buying in bulk. On negotiation it gives an example: for a $10 unit, offering $7 or $8 on a 1,000-unit order is reasonable, while offering $2 is not. Suppliers often sell samples at the retail price. claim: Set the pre-shipment inspection at AQL 2.5 for general consumer goods with zero critical defects: for 4,000 units at General Inspection Level II, sample 200 and accept the lot only if 10 or fewer fail.
body: QIMA, an inspection company, explains Acceptable Quality Limit sampling, based on ISO 2859 and ANSI/ASQ Z1.4. AQL sets the most defective units a random sample may contain before the whole lot is rejected, and is set separately for each defect type. QIMA says AQL for critical defects (safety or legal failures) is commonly 0; AQL 2.5 is the most common standard for general consumer goods; AQL 1.0 is used for higher-risk categories; and AQL 4.0 where minor cosmetic defects are acceptable. Its worked example: a shipment of 4,000 units inspected at General Inspection Level II gives code letter L; code letter L at AQL 2.5 calls for a sample of 200 units; if 10 or fewer fail the batch passes, and 11 or more means rejection. The value of agreeing these numbers is that pass and fail are defined before production, so a failed inspection is a contract matter, not an argument. How to apply: write the AQL levels (0 critical, 2.5 major, 4.0 minor, or stricter for children's or electrical products) and the defect list into the purchase order, and book the inspection before the final payment.
conditions: Bulk production runs from contract factories; random sampling of finished goods.

claim: In the US, any product designed mainly for children 12 or younger needs a Children's Product Certificate based on tests by a CPSC-accepted third-party lab, and importers must e-file certificates from 8 July 2026.

A children's product is a consumer product designed or intended primarily for children 12 years of age or younger, and those subject to a children's product safety rule need third-party testing and certification. The certificate has seven elements: the product covered, each applicable safety rule, the manufacturer or importer, contact details for whoever keeps the test records, date and place of manufacture, date and place of testing, and the lab (or a small-batch registration number). This adds lab fees, time and paperwork to every children's product idea, and the costs repeat with material or supplier changes. claim: At the idea stage, look up the US duty rate in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule or the USITC database, treat it as approximate since CBP makes the final call, and get a binding ruling when the margin depends on it.
body: US Customs and Border Protection's guidance on duty rates says the Harmonized Tariff Schedule gives duty rates for virtually every item, but classifying an item correctly takes expertise: details such as fibre content, construction and country of origin change the rate. The USITC Tariff Database gives an approximate rate, only as accurate as the information entered. CBP makes the final determination of the correct duty rate, not the importer, and for very specific duty information on a particular item an importer can request a binding ruling; local ports can also advise. For a product idea, duty is one of the few landed-cost lines that can move the margin by many points, and additional duties on top of the base rate can apply by origin, so a guess made from a similar product can be wrong. How to apply: for each shortlisted idea, find the likely HTS code and base duty, check for additional duties for the planned origin country, add duty to the landed cost on the cautious side, and for any product where a different code would break the margin, request a binding ruling before the first order.

body: Jungle Scout's 2024 seller report surveyed nearly 2,000 Amazon sellers and businesses between 1 December 2023 and 3 January 2024, focusing on 1,064 sellers with at least one live listing. Among small and mid-size sellers, 57% reported profit margins higher than 10%, 28% above 20%, and 13% said the business was not yet profitable. On timing, 22% were profitable within three months, 16% in three to six months, 20% in six months to a year, 11% in one to two years and 2% after more than two years, so 58% were profitable within the first year. They are useful as a reality check on a plan: a model that assumes a margin well above 20% from month one sits above what most sellers report. How to apply: when building the plan for a new product, treat roughly 10% to 20% net margin as the normal range, show the month the product turns profitable, and test the plan at a margin below 10% to see whether the cash still lasts.

claim: Jungle Scout's seller survey found 31% of Amazon sellers made under $500 a month and 17% $501 to $1,000; only small shares reached $25,000 or more, so a typical new product sells far less than the leaders.
body: Jungle Scout's 2024 report, from a survey of nearly 2,000 Amazon sellers and businesses (1,064 with a live listing), gives the spread of monthly sales: under $500, 31%; $501 to $1,000, 17%; $1,001 to $5,000, 22%; $5,001 to $10,000, 11%; $10,001 to $25,000, 7%; $25,001 to $50,000, 5%; $50,001 to $100,000, 4%; and 1% each in the two bands above $100,000. On start-up spend, 25% spent under $1,000 and 64% under $5,000, with 17% spending more than $10,000. The point for product research is base rates: the revenue figures that research tools show for top listings describe the leaders, while most sellers sit far below them. A demand estimate taken from the top three listings in a niche is the ceiling, not the expected result. How to apply: when forecasting a new product, model a base case well below the niche leaders' monthly revenue, size the first order to that base case, and treat leader-level sales as the upside to reorder into.
conditions: Amazon sellers, mostly US, surveyed December 2023 to January 2024.
numbers: 31% under $500 a month
64% spent under $5,000 to start

claim: In Jungle Scout's January 2025 survey of nearly 1,500 Amazon sellers, 38% named higher shipping costs as a top challenge, 34% rising cost of goods and 32% growing ad costs: stress-test every idea's margin on all three.
body: Jungle Scout's State of the Amazon Seller 2025 surveyed nearly 1,500 Amazon sellers and businesses from 10 to 27 January 2025. The top challenges were cost pressures: 38% cited higher shipping costs, 34% said they struggled with the rising cost of goods, and 32% said growing advertising expenses were a concern. The report also says fewer businesses source from China while sourcing from the US has nearly doubled, without giving exact shares. For product research this argues for testing margins against cost increases rather than today's quotes: freight, unit cost and click prices are the three lines most sellers saw rise, and a product with a thin margin at current costs is the first to break. How to apply: for each shortlisted idea, rerun the unit economics with freight, landed unit cost and cost per click each raised by a set stress amount, and drop ideas whose margin turns negative under the combined case; favour ideas whose price can absorb increases without leaving the niche's price band.
conditions: Amazon sellers, survey January 2025.

claim: In the US, a general-use product covered by a CPSC safety rule needs a General Certificate of Conformity from its maker or importer, based on testing or a reasonable testing program; third-party lab testing is not required.
body: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission's page on the General Certificate of Conformity says domestic manufacturers and importers of certain general-use products, meaning products not made primarily for children, must issue a written certificate under section 14(a) of the Consumer Product Safety Act when the product is subject to a CPSC rule or similar requirement. The certificate must be based on testing or a reasonable testing program; unlike children's products, third-party laboratory testing is not required, though a certifier that relies on a third-party lab must name it. The certificate has seven elements: the product, each CPSC rule it is certified to, the certifying manufacturer or importer, contact details for whoever keeps the test records, date and place of manufacture, date and place of testing, and any third-party lab used. From 8 July 2026 importers of most regulated consumer products must file certificates electronically with US Customs and Border Protection. For a private label importer, the importer is the certifier, not the factory. How to apply: for each idea, check whether any CPSC rule covers the product type; if one does, plan who tests, budget for it in the landed cost, and have the certificate ready before the first shipment is entered.
conditions: General-use (non-children's) consumer products imported into or made in the US and covered by a CPSC rule.
numbers: seven certificate elements
e-filing from 8 July 2026
